Last unit you found the parts all cells share, so now the question is why cells end up looking so different from each other.

## Engage: same DNA?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students who think different cells have different DNA will choose that; specialisation by using different instructions is the idea the node needs."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A nerve cell and a muscle cell from the same person. How do you predict their DNA compares?"
  options: ["Completely different DNA", "The same DNA, but each cell uses different parts of it", "Muscle cells have more DNA", "Only nerve cells have DNA"]
  actual: "The same DNA. Each cell switches on the instructions it needs, so it grows the shape and parts that suit its job."
```

## Explore: four specialised cells

```step
stage: run
insight: "Clicking each feature and reading its purpose links structure to function cell by cell."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#blood", height: 520 }
tasks:
  - starter: "boards.yml#blood"
    check: { type: board, text: "Find every part of the red blood cell and the nerve cell.", when: "n = k" }
    hint: ["Every branch, bump and band is a part, so work along the nerve cell from one end to the other.", "The line under the board counts what you've found, so if it isn't full, try the thin lines and the middle of the red blood cell."]
  - starter: "boards.yml#muscle"
    check: { type: board, text: "Find every part of the muscle cell and the root hair cell.", when: "n = k" }
    hint: ["Some parts are small and there are several of them, so click one of each kind and read its name under the board.", "If the count isn't full, try the thin outlines of both cells and the long part sticking out of the root hair cell."]
```

## Explain: shape suits job

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Explaining features as adaptations, not labels, is the hinge for tissues and organs."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each feature to how it helps."
      pairs:
        - ["Red blood cell: no nucleus", "More room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen"]
        - ["Nerve cell: long axon", "Carries signals a long way"]
        - ["Muscle cell: many mitochondria", "Releases lots of energy for contracting"]
        - ["Root hair cell: long extension", "Large surface for absorbing water"]
    hint: ["Take each feature and finish the sentence 'so that the cell can…'.", "Click each feature on the board again and read what it's for in the line that comes up."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why do root hair cells have no chloroplasts?"
      options: ["They are underground, where there is no light for photosynthesis", "Roots take in their food from the soil, so they don't need to make any", "Only leaves are allowed chloroplasts"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Soil gives water and minerals, not food: root cells get sugar from the leaves through the phloem. What do chloroplasts need that roots don't get?", "The DNA for chloroplasts is there; root cells don't switch it on because there is no light."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What does 'specialised' mean for a cell?"
      options: ["Its shape and parts suit one particular job", "It has different DNA", "It is bigger than other cells"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Same DNA: different instructions used.", "Size varies; it's the match to the job that counts."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I described two features of a specialised cell and explained how each helps it do its job." }
```

## Elaborate: design a cell

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Predicting the features a job needs reverses the reasoning: function to structure."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Cells lining your small intestine absorb digested food. Which feature would you expect them to have?"
  options: ["Tiny folds (microvilli) on the surface, for a much larger area", "No membrane, so food gets in easily", "A long tail to swim"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Without a membrane, everything would leak out.", "They stay put; the food comes to them."]
  explain: "Like root hairs, intestine cells increase their surface area to absorb more."
```

## Elaborate: energy-hungry cells

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Comparing organelle numbers across cells extends specialisation from shape to contents."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Sperm cells and muscle cells both have many mitochondria. What do the two jobs have in common?"
  options: ["Both need lots of energy for movement", "Both make proteins", "Both store food"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Ribosomes make proteins.", "Neither is a food store."]
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the DNA of nerve and muscle cells with what I now know." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- Nearly all your cells have the **same DNA**; each **specialised** cell uses different instructions.
- A specialised cell's **shape and parts suit its job**: red blood cells (no nucleus, haemoglobin), nerve cells (long axon), muscle cells (many mitochondria), root hair cells (long extension, no chloroplasts).

```teacher
summary: Students explain that cells with the same DNA specialise, and describe
  how structural features of specialised cells serve their functions (AC9S8U02,
  node 1, a hinge node).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 9 min · Explain 8 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical adds
  2 min, Wider about 2 min
goals:
  - I can describe two features of a specialised cell and explain how each helps.
  - I can explain that cells with the same DNA can specialise for different jobs.
  - I can link a cell's contents (such as mitochondria) to its job.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace
  prepared slides of blood, nerve and muscle tissue. Set the width with
  `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or `wider`.


  The hinge is the structure-function link. Students who list features without
  the "so that" cannot reason about tissues and organs.


  Board notes: diagrams are simplified and not to scale (a nerve cell's axon can
  be a metre long).
running:
  - "Engage: the 'different DNA' choice is the misconception to resolve."
  - "Explore: after each cell, ask for one feature and its 'so that'."
  - "Explain: the match covers four cells; the root hair question returns to the
    DNA idea."
struggle: Linking each feature to its job ('so that…'). When a student lists
  features, ask 'so that what?'
stuck:
  - see: A student says red blood cells lost their nucleus by accident.
    ask: What gets more room without it?
    fix: Haemoglobin, so it carries more oxygen. It's a feature, not damage.
  - see: A student lists features without functions.
    ask: So that what?
    fix: "Each feature: '…, so that the cell can …'."
stretch: Stem cells can become many types of cell. Why might that be useful in medicine?
support: "A frame: 'The ___ cell has ___ so that it can ___.'"
leads: >
  Next: tissues (node 2), then organs built from tissues (node 3).


  In class: prepared slides of blood smear, muscle and nerve tissue; a
  cheek-cell versus onion-cell comparison.
exit:
  q: Give one feature of a nerve cell and explain how it helps.
  a: A long axon, so it can carry signals a long way through the body.
explain: >
  Cells with the same DNA **specialise**: each develops a shape and parts that
  suit its job. Red blood cells have no nucleus (more haemoglobin); nerve cells
  have long axons; muscle cells have many mitochondria; root hair cells have a
  long extension.
```
